hints: Think about the colour of the excess reactant gas and the physical state of the phosphorus chloride product at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Picture the starting materials**
You have solid phosphorus reacting with excess chlorine gas. Chlorine is a distinctive pale green gas, so at the start the reaction vessel looks green.

Track what is used up and made**
As reaction 1 proceeds, the green $\text{Cl}_{2}$ is consumed to make $\text{PCl}_{5}$. $\text{PCl}_{5}$ is a white solid that often appears as white smoke or fumes in moist air. So you see the green colour disappear and a white solid appear.
Final answer: Green gas fades / decolourises and white solid / white fumes formed.

hints: Focus on the reagent in reaction 2, water, reacting with a chloride to give an acid and HCl.
walkthrough:
Recognise the signature of water splitting a compound**
In reaction 2, $\text{PCl}_{5}$ reacts with $\text{H}_{2}\text{O}$ to give $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ and $\text{HCl}$. Whenever water breaks down a covalent chloride in this way, forming an acid, we call it hydrolysis.
Final answer: Hydrolysis.

hints: Assign oxidation numbers first, remember free element P is 0, O is -1 in most compounds except peroxides, and H is +1.
Look for one element whose number increases (loss of electrons) and another whose number decreases (gain of electrons) in the same equation.
walkthrough:
Work out the oxidation numbers**
Free phosphorus, $\text{P}$, is $0$. In $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$, $3(+1) + P + 4(-2) = 0$, so $P = +5$. In $\text{HNO}_{3}$, $+1 + N + 3(-2) = 0$, so $N = +5$. In $\text{NO}_{2}$, $N + 2(-2) = 0$, so $N = +4$.

Link change to oxidation and reduction**
Phosphorus goes from $0$ to $+5$. That is an increase, meaning loss of electrons, so phosphorus is oxidised. Nitrogen goes from $+5$ to $+4$. That is a decrease, meaning gain of electrons, so nitrogen is reduced.

Conclude redox**
Because one species is oxidised and another is reduced in the same reaction, this must be a redox reaction.

Final answer: P: 0 in P to +5 in $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$, oxidised (increase in oxidation number).
N: +5 in $\text{HNO}_{3}$ to +4 in $\text{NO}_{2}$, reduced (decrease in oxidation number).
Both oxidation and reduction occur, so redox.

hints: Recall the two AS definitions of a base and look at what happens to $\text{NH}_{3}$ when it becomes $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$.
walkthrough:
See the change from ammonia to ammonium**
In reaction 3, $\text{NH}_{3}$ becomes $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$. The only difference is one extra $\text{H}^{+}$. That $\text{H}^{+}$ must have come from the acid $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$. Accepting a proton is exactly what a Bronsted-Lowry base does. In Lewis terms, the nitrogen uses its lone pair to form the new N-H dative bond.
Final answer: $\text{NH}_{3}$ accepts a proton / $\text{H}^{+}$ from $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ to form $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ (or donates its lone pair of electrons).

hints: Count bonding pairs and lone pairs on N in $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$ and compare with methane to predict shape.
walkthrough:
Count the electron pairs around nitrogen**
In $\text{NH}_{4}^{+}$, nitrogen has four bonding pairs and zero lone pairs. Four pairs repel equally to get as far apart as possible.

Name the shape and angle**
Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs always gives a tetrahedral arrangement, just like $\text{CH}_{4}$. Draw N in the centre with one wedge bond coming out, one dashed bond going back, and two normal bonds, with all H-N-H angles $109.5^{\circ}$.
Final answer: Tetrahedral 3-D shape with four N-H bonds (wedge and dashed bonds shown) and bond angle $109.5^{\circ}$.

hints: Think what elements plants need for growth that are present in $(\text{NH}_{4}^{+})(\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}^{-})$.
walkthrough:
Spot the plant nutrients**
$(\text{NH}_{4}^{+})(\text{H}_{2}\text{PO}_{4}^{-})$ contains both nitrogen and phosphorus, two of the three essential elements for plant growth (N, P, K). Ammonium phosphates are therefore manufactured on a large scale as fertilisers.
Final answer: Used as fertilisers.

hints: Remember $\text{PCl}_{5}$ replaces the OH group by Cl, and the other products contain P, O and H with Cl.
walkthrough:
Balance the conversion**
The OH group in ethanol is replaced by Cl to give $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$. The remaining O, H and PCl atoms form phosphorus oxychloride and hydrogen chloride: $$\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH} + \text{PCl}_{5} \rightarrow \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl} + \text{POCl}_{3} + \text{HCl}$$ Check atoms balance on both sides.

hints: Identify which group leaves the carbon and which atom takes its place.
walkthrough:
See the swap at carbon**
The $\text{OH}$ group on $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{OH}$ is directly swapped for $\text{Cl}$ to give $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$. One group substitutes for another, so this is a substitution reaction.
Final answer: Substitution.

hints: Compare the reducing power of $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$ and think which halide ion is more easily oxidised.
Consider the oxidising ability of concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ versus concentrated $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ toward that halide.
walkthrough:
Compare halide reducing strength**
Iodide, $\text{I}^{-}$, is a much stronger reducing agent than chloride, $\text{Cl}^{-}$, because the larger iodide ion loses electrons more easily.

See why sulfuric acid fails**
Concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ is a strong enough oxidising agent to oxidise $\text{HI}$ / $\text{I}^{-}$ to iodine, $\text{I}_{2}$. So instead of getting pure $\text{HI}$, you get contamination with $\text{I}_{2}$ plus $\text{SO}_{2}$ and other reduction products.

See why phosphoric acid works**
Concentrated $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ is not an oxidising agent, so it simply provides $\text{H}^{+}$ to make $\text{HI}$ from $\text{NaI}$ without further oxidation.

Final answer: $\text{HI}$ / $\text{I}^{-}$ is a stronger reducing agent than $\text{HCl}$ / $\text{Cl}^{-}$ and is oxidised by concentrated $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ to $\text{I}_{2}$, so $\text{HI}$ is not obtained. Concentrated $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ is not an oxidising agent so does not oxidise $\text{I}^{-}$.

hints: Order the three halogenoalkanes from fastest to slowest hydrolysis with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$.
Think about which C-X bond breaks during hydrolysis and how bond length and strength change from Cl to I.
walkthrough:
State the observed order**
When warmed separately with $\text{NaOH(aq)}$, $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{I}$ hydrolyses fastest and $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$ slowest: $$\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl} < \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Br} < \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{I}$$

Link rate to bond breaking**
Hydrolysis involves breaking the C-X bond. Bond strength decreases down the group because the atoms get larger and overlap gets poorer. So C-Cl is strongest and shortest, C-I is weakest and longest.

Explain the energy link**
The weaker the C-X bond, the less energy needed to break it, so hydrolysis is faster. That is why the iodoalkane reacts fastest.

Final answer: Reactivity: $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl} < \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Br} < \text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{I}$, fastest is $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{I}$, slowest is $\text{C}_{2}\text{H}_{5}\text{Cl}$.
C-I is weakest and C-Cl is strongest, so C-I breaks most easily and requires least energy.
